### Season outlook as written in the guide (p. 178)

Bob Chesney has been a rising star in the coaching ranks for several years now after leading Holy Cross to the FCS Playoffs five times in seven years and then getting James Madison into the College Football Playoff just two seasons after Curt Cignetti left for Indiana. Like Cignetti, Chesney brings a lot of his staff (eight assistants) with him to his new home from JMU including offensive coordinator Dean Kennedy and defensive coordinator Colin Hitschler. He also brings in 10 of his 42 transfers from James Madison. However, it is the player who is staying that is the starting point, as quarterback Nico Iamaleava returns to work with a new staff that led James Madison to the No. 16 offense (452.6 yards per game) in the nation. Under 6.5 They are clearly hoping that history repeats itself in Westwood with what Cignetti did in Bloomington. Chesney is a good coach and he and his staff are a massive upgrade over Deshaun Foster and his group, and he has a chance to turn this around at UCLA, but this team is still a bit overpriced. The non- conference slate, especially with games at Cal and vs. San Diego State are not gimme wins. While they avoid Ohio State and Indiana, the Bruins still have trips to Michigan and Oregon. A 6-6 campaign is certainly realistic, but getting to seven wins seems to be a reach with so many new faces and so many unproven positions.

## 26. Open Questions / Risks

The guide's *Three Burning Questions for the 2026 Season* *(p. 179)*, with the answers as written:

### Is Nico Iamaleava ready to take the next step?

After all the drama surrounding his transfer from Tennessee, Iamaleava had a disappointing inaugural campaign in Westwood, throwing for just 1,929 yards in 11 starts. However, he did complete 64.4% of his passes and only threw seven interceptions while adding 505 yards and four touchdowns on the ground. Chesney brings him some help from James Madison including all-purpose running back Wayne Knight (1,373 rush yards, nine TDs; 397 rec yards, one TD) to go along with returning backs Jaivian Thomas and Anthony Woods, plus three offensive line starters Riley Robell, Carter Sweezie (both All-Sun Belt), and JD Rayner. Essentially a brand-new receiving corps joins holdover Mikey Matthews (33-348- 2) with Landon Ellis (James Madison), Leland Smith (San Jose State), Brian Rowe (South Carolina), Aidan Mizell (Florida), and Semaj Morgan (Michigan) entering the fold.

### Can a true No. 1 wide receiver emerge?

One of the reasons for Iamaleava’s disappointing passing numbers is because the wide receivers did not give much help. Nico is a playmaker that is most effective throwing on the run instead of standing in the pocket, so receivers must get some separation. Rowe, from South Carolina, is the most talented of the group. Ellis (624 yards) has familiarity with the offense from his time at James Madison. Smith (43-688-3) posted good numbers at San Jose State.

### Can the defensive line get some pressure on opposing quarterbacks?

No team in FBS was worse in doing so than UCLA last season, as they only registered 10 sacks. Chesney did go into the transfer portal and brought in key players like Sun Belt Freshman of the Year Sahir West (seven sacks) and Aiden Gobaira (four sacks) from James Madison. Oklahoma transfer linebacker Samuel Omosigho (50 tackles, two sacks). The talented secondary masked a lot of the defensive line’s weaknesses last year and it will be a talented group in the back again, but the defensive line must help them out up front or the Bruins will give plenty of points just like last year (33.4 PPG, 125th nationally).
